message.content:
**Plasma‑Membrane Proteins – A Quick Reference** | Category | Typical Function | Representative Examples | |----------|------------------|-------------------------| | **Integral (Transmembrane) Proteins** | Span the lipid bilayer; often act as gates, pumps, or signal receivers. | • Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase
• Glucose transporter GLUT1
• Aquaporin‑2
• Rhodopsin (photoreceptor)
• G‑protein–coupled receptors (e.g., β₂‑adrenergic receptor)
• Ion channels (voltage‑gated K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻)
• Connexin hemichannels (gap junctions)
• Integrins (αβ heterodimers)
• Cadherins (calcium‑dependent adhesion)
• Tetraspanins (CD9, CD63) | | **Peripheral Membrane Proteins** | Associate loosely via electrostatic interactions or through covalent attachment to lipids. | • Spectrin (cytoskeletal scaffold)
• Actin (linker to membrane complexes)
• Annexins (phospholipid binding)
• Protein kinase C (binds phosphatidylserine)
• Myristoylated Src family kinases (anchor to inner leaflet) | | **Lipid‑Anchored Proteins** | Covalently tethered to one side of the bilayer via fatty acid chains. | • Prenylated Ras (C‑terminal CAAX motif)
• Palmitoylated GAP43 (neuronal growth cone marker)
• N‑myristoyl‑glycine‑modified Lyn kinase | | **Extracellular Matrix / Adhesion Molecules** | Extend into the extracellular space to mediate cell–matrix contacts. | • Fibronectin (integrin ligand)
• Collagen IV (basement membrane component)
• Heparan sulfate proteoglycans (syndecans) | ### How These Proteins Work Together * **Signal Transduction:** GPCRs bind ligands → activate intracellular G‑proteins → downstream effectors (adenylyl cyclase, PLC). * **Transport & Homeostasis:** Ion pumps maintain gradients; glucose transporters allow nutrient uptake. * **Cell Communication & Structure:** Gap junctions permit ionic coupling; adherens junctions stabilize tissue architecture. --- #### Quick Tips If You Want More Detail: 1. **Look up “plasma membrane proteome” datasets** from resources like UniProt or Human Protein Atlas—these catalog thousands of identified proteins. 2. For *specific tissues*, check specialized databases (e.g., BrainAtlas for neuronal membranes). 3. Use bioinformatics tools (BLAST, Pfam) to identify domain architectures typical of membrane proteins (transmembrane helix predictions, glycosylation sites). Feel free to ask about particular families, subtypes, or how certain mutations affect their function!
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What are the names of proteins found in the plasma membrane?" They likely expect an answer listing some common types or examples of plasma membrane proteins.

We can provide general categories: integral membrane proteins such as receptors, transporters, ion channels; peripheral membrane proteins etc. Provide example names: Na+/K+ ATPase, GLUT1, Rhodopsin, G-protein coupled receptor, integrins, cadherins, connexins, aquaporins, transferrin receptor, CD molecules, etc.

Also mention classification: transmembrane helices vs beta-barrel. Could also give references.

Thus produce concise but informative response. No need to call tool.
